lessons.title: Preparing for a field inspection
lessons.html:
Preparing for a field inspection

Seed production fields, called seed units, are inspected during the season to check that the crop meets the standards for the class of seed being produced. The field inspection looks at things that cannot be checked in the laboratory later, such as isolation from other crops, off-type plants in the field and, in hybrids, correct pollination control. Certification schemes in South Africa run under the Plant Improvement Act, and SANSOR acts as the designated authority for many crops.

Information you need

  • Registration details: grower, farm, unit number, crop, cultivar, class, area and planting date.
  • A map or GPS location of the unit and its boundaries.
  • The parent seed details, such as label numbers.
  • The standards for the crop and class: isolation distance, maximum off-types, other crops and weeds, and the required number and timing of inspections.
  • The official cultivar description, so you know what true-to-type plants look like.

Timing

Inspections must take place at the stages where problems can be seen. For example, in hybrid maize, inspections during flowering are critical to check detasselling of female rows and pollen shedders. In self-pollinated crops such as wheat and soybeans, off-types are often easiest to see near flowering or maturity, when height, flower colour and pod or ear differences show.

Equipment

  • Inspection forms or tablet, clipboard, pens
  • GPS, measuring wheel or rangefinder
  • Tally counter, tape measure, sample bags, labels
  • Hat, water, sunscreen, boots, long sleeves

Arrange the visit with the grower and ask about recent spraying. Do not enter a field within the re-entry period on a product label. Be aware of hazards such as snakes, bees, irrigation pivots and farm machinery.

lessons.title: Inspecting the seed unit and corrective action
lessons.html:
Inspecting the seed unit and corrective action

Inspecting surroundings

  • Drive or walk the boundary and look for other fields of the same crop, volunteer plants and weedy edges.
  • Measure distances to possible contamination sources and compare with the isolation standard.
  • Note any differences between the field and the map, such as an extra block planted.

Inspecting inside the unit

  1. Enter the field and follow the counting pattern in the scheme rules, spread across the whole unit.
  2. At each count point, examine the set number of plants. Record off-types, other cultivars, other crop plants and specified weeds.
  3. In hybrid fields, check male and female rows, detasselling quality, pollen shedders in female rows and the timing of male pollen shed versus female silking.
  4. Look at overall crop condition: disease, pests, weeds, lodging and uniformity.
  5. Mark problem areas with GPS points.

Corrective action

If the unit does not meet standards but the problem can be fixed, the inspector gives instructions for corrective action:

ProblemTypical corrective action
Off-types above standardRogue (pull out and remove) off-type plants, then re-inspect
Poor detassellingRepeat detasselling at once
Isolation failure near a borderRemove the affected border strip from the seed unit
Specified weedsRemove weeds before they set seed

Give instructions clearly in writing, with a date for re-inspection. Show the grower or farm manager the problem areas. Some problems cannot be fixed, for example serious isolation failure across the whole unit, and lead to rejection.

lessons.title: Completing the inspection process
lessons.html:
Completing the inspection process

The inspection report is the official record that decides whether the seed from this unit can continue towards certification. It must be accurate, complete and submitted on time.

Writing the report

  • Record unit details, inspection date, crop stage and weather.
  • Record isolation findings with distances.
  • Record counts at each count point and the calculated levels of off-types, other crops and weeds.
  • Record the decision: pass, conditional (corrective action and re-inspection), partial rejection or rejection.
  • Record corrective instructions and the re-inspection date.
  • Sign and date the report.

Re-inspection

Return on the agreed date and check that corrective action was done properly. Count again. If the unit now meets standards, record a pass. If not, the unit may be rejected. Record everything as on the first visit.

Submitting and filing

  1. Submit reports to the certification authority and the seed company within the required time.
  2. Give the grower a copy of the findings.
  3. File copies for the period your procedure requires.

Professional conduct

Growers depend on their seed contracts for income, and a rejected unit can cost them a lot of money. Explain your findings with facts and show them the evidence. Stay polite and firm. Never change a result because of pressure or gifts. If there is a dispute, refer it to your manager and the certification authority.

After the field stage

A unit that passes the field inspection still has to be harvested cleanly, processed and tested in the laboratory before certified labels are issued. Pass on any concerns, such as disease seen in the field, to the processing and laboratory teams.

Key points

  • Field inspections check isolation, off-types and pollination control that a laboratory cannot see later.
  • Prepare with registration details, standards, cultivar description and the right crop stage.
  • Follow the official counting pattern across the whole unit.
  • Give clear written corrective actions and re-inspect.
  • Report accurately, on time and with integrity.

quiz.question: Why are seed units inspected in the field?

options.text: To check things the laboratory cannot see later, such as isolation and off-types

quiz.question: In hybrid maize, which stage is critical for inspection?

options.text: Pulling out and removing off-type plants

quiz.question: There is an isolation failure near one border only. What is a typical corrective action?

options.text: Remove the affected border strip from the unit

quiz.question: What should you do if a grower disputes your findings?

options.text: Change the result to keep them happy
Refer it to your manager and the certification authority
